item.research_question: Can a novel equiatomic CrMoNbTiZr high-entropy alloy (HEA) be synthesized and exhibit suitable properties for biomedical applications?
item.processing_route: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C with a heating rate of 100 °C/min and a holding time of 15 min under a uniaxial pressure of 40 MPa
item.test_conditions: Room temperature compression tests, potentiodynamic polarization in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) and Hanks' solutions, and wear tests against an alumina ball
key_findings: The alloy exhibited a relative density of 97% of the theoretical density
The microstructure consisted primarily of BCC and Laves phases
The global Vickers microhardness was 531.5 ± 99.7 HV
The ultimate compressive strength and compressive yield strength were 1235.7 ± 42.8 MPa and 1110.8 ± 78.6 MPa, respectively
The elasticity modulus was 34.9 ± 3.1 GPa, within the range reported for cortical bone
The alloy exhibited good bio-corrosion resistance with low current densities in PBS and Hanks' solutions
The average coefficient of friction (COF) was 0.43 ± 0.06, characterized mainly by abrasive and adhesive wear mechanisms
item.mechanism: The high microhardness and compressive properties of the alloy can be attributed to the presence of BCC and Laves phases, while the low elasticity modulus is beneficial for minimizing stress-shielding or loosening of implants
item.limitations: Further research is required to investigate the fretting wear behavior and assess other in vitro and in vivo cell proliferation properties of the alloy
item.future_work: Investigation of fretting wear behavior and in vitro and in vivo cell proliferation properties
quotes: The microstructure consisted primarily of BCC and Laves phases, which matched the prediction from a thermodynamic CALPHAD simulation

records.text: Paper card. Question: Can a novel equiatomic CrMoNbTiZr high-entropy alloy (HEA) be synthesized and exhibit suitable properties for biomedical applications?. System: CrMoNbTiZr high-entropy alloy. Processing: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C with a heating rate of 100 °C/min and a holding time of 15 min under a uniaxial pressure of 40 MPa. Test conditions: Room temperature compression tests, potentiodynamic polarization in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) and Hanks' solutions, and wear tests against an alumina ball. Findings: The alloy exhibited a relative density of 97% of the theoretical density; The microstructure consisted primarily of BCC and Laves phases; The global Vickers microhardness was 531.5 ± 99.7 HV; The ultimate compressive strength and compressive yield strength were 1235.7 ± 42.8 MPa and 1110.8 ± 78.6 MPa, respectively; The elasticity modulus was 34.9 ± 3.1 GPa, within the range reported for cortical bone; The alloy exhibited good bio-corrosion resistance with low current densities in PBS and Hanks' solutions; The average coefficient of friction (COF) was 0.43 ± 0.06, characterized mainly by abrasive and adhesive wear mechanisms. Mechanism: The high microhardness and compressive properties of the alloy can be attributed to the presence of BCC and Laves phases, while the low elasticity modulus is beneficial for minimizing stress-shielding or loosening of implants. Limitations: Further research is required to investigate the fretting wear behavior and assess other in vitro and in vivo cell proliferation properties of the alloy. Future work: Investigation of fretting wear behavior and in vitro and in vivo cell proliferation properties.
